summary: For ages 9–11: how the three plate-boundary motions (convergent/pushing together, divergent/pulling apart, transform/sliding past) each produce different hazards and landforms, so the TYPE of motion predicts what you get. The load-bearing idea is that if everything else stays the same and only the motion changes, the results change: collisions build mountains, and where a denser ocean plate dives under another (subduction) you get volcanoes that are often explosive; spreading opens ridges with new crust, gentler volcanism and mostly smaller earthquakes; sliding can cause big earthquakes, usually with no volcano. Earthquakes happen at all three types. When plates push together, the kind of crust (ocean or continent) also affects what forms. Activities centre on enacting the motion and predicting the result before revealing it, then anchoring each rule to a real place (Himalayas, Mid-Atlantic Ridge, San Andreas). This operationalises WHY earthquakes and volcanoes cluster in bands along boundaries.
misconceptions: Every plate boundary produces both volcanoes and earthquakes in the same way (the type of motion determines which hazards/landforms occur).
Mountains are pushed up by volcanoes only (many great ranges form by plate COLLISION crumpling crust, without volcanoes).
At divergent boundaries the plates leave a permanent empty gap (new crust forms from rising magma to fill the spreading gap).
Transform boundaries make volcanoes (they mainly cause earthquakes as plates grind past — usually no volcanism).
Boundaries are single thin lines with no width (they are zones where deformation, quakes and volcanism spread over a region).

activities.title: Drive one boundary, three ways: predict then see the result
steps: Work with a single boundary between two plates that has a motion selector: PUSH (together), PULL (apart), SLIDE (past).
Before running each motion, write or say a prediction: 'If I push these plates together, I think I'll get ___.'

Run PUSH and watch the crust buckle and crumple upward into a mountain range; in a second case, where a denser ocean plate meets another plate, watch it dive under, heat up and release water so that rock above it partly melts, and a volcano (often explosive) grow.
Run PULL and watch a ridge crack open with magma welling up to make brand-new ground and gentle volcanism.
Run SLIDE and watch the plates lock, stress build, and SNAP into a big earthquake — with no volcano.
Attach real-place tags as you experiment: Himalayas (collision), Mid-Atlantic Ridge (spreading), San Andreas (sliding).
State the big insight in your own words: in this model, the same two plates give different results when only the way they move is changed (in real places, the kind of crust also matters).
activities.insight: Boundary TYPE (the kind of motion) predicts the hazard and landform; it is not that every boundary does the same thing. Convergent → mountains / subduction volcanoes / deep quakes; divergent → ridge, new crust, gentle volcanism, mostly smaller shallow quakes; transform → big earthquakes, usually no volcano. Earthquakes happen at all three; at convergent boundaries, the kind of crust decides whether you mainly get collision mountains or subduction volcanoes.

activities.title: Hands-on plate models with everyday materials
steps: Enact pushing together, pulling apart, and sliding past using foam blocks, your two hands, or biscuits/graham crackers resting on a soft filling (e.g. frosting).
Crumple two sheets of paper or two rugs by pushing them together to raise a ridge — model how collision crumples crust into mountains.

For subduction, push two blocks together and let one slide under the other; describe how the diving plate heats up and releases water, which makes the hot rock above it partly melt, feeding magma that rises to a volcano.
Name each motion only after you have physically done it, then predict what hazard or landform it would create.
activities.insight: The abstract motions become physical actions, and the collision→mountains and subduction→volcano links become something the learner has built with their hands before naming.

activities.title: Labelled cross-sections with reveal and drill-down
steps: Study three labelled side-view cross-sections: convergent (collision/subduction), divergent (spreading ridge), transform (sliding past).
Tap or lift a flap on each to reveal its motion, its hazards/landforms, and a real example.
Answer targeted reveal prompts such as 'Which boundary makes mountains without volcanoes?' (collision) before checking.
Drill into the subduction diagram to see one plate diving and releasing water at depth, rock above it partly melting, and magma rising.
activities.insight: A clear reference mapping of motion→result across all three boundary types, with the subduction mechanism made explicit.

activities.title: Consolidate and sort: match, categorize, sequence
steps: Match each boundary type to its hazard/landform.
Categorize real places by boundary type: sort Himalayas (collision), Iceland/Mid-Atlantic Ridge (spreading), San Andreas (sliding).
Sequence a subduction chain in order: plate dives → heats up and releases water → rock above it partly melts → magma rises → volcano erupts.

Answer the diagnostic: 'At one place two plates push together; at another they slide past. A friend says it doesn't matter how plates meet — you get the same thing everywhere. Do you agree? What differs depending on HOW they meet?'
activities.insight: Secure recall and correct application of the motion→feature rules, and explicit rejection of the 'same everywhere' idea by explaining what differs by motion type.

activities.title: Extension: 3D block model of subduction and collision
steps: If available, manipulate a 3D plate-block model you can push, pull, and slide, and rotate to view from any angle.
Look along the depth of the model to see a subducting plate diving beneath another.
Compare the 3D depth view with the 2D cross-sections you used earlier and describe what each view shows more clearly.
activities.insight: Subduction and collision happen in three dimensions; a depth view can make the diving plate easier to picture, complementing the cross-section view.

checkQuestion: At one place two plates are pushing together; at another they're sliding past each other. A friend says, 'It doesn't matter how the plates meet — you get the same thing everywhere.' Do you agree? What happens differently depending on HOW the plates meet at a boundary?
checkAnswer: The friend is wrong — what happens depends on how the plates move. Where they push together (convergent) you get mountains, and one plate can slide under another and melt to feed volcanoes; where they pull apart (divergent) magma rises to make new crust and volcanoes; where they slide past (transform) you mainly get earthquakes. The type of movement controls the features.
